title: Kangana Ranaut's 26/11 Film Tells the Story Nobody Made for 18 Years. It Opens Thursday.
excerpt: Bharat Bhagya Vidhata recreates the night nurses at Mumbai's Cama Hospital saved 400 lives while terrorists moved through the corridors. Delhi has already declared it tax-free.
body:
Everyone remembers the Taj. The Trident. Leopold Café. The images of smoke billowing from South Mumbai's most iconic buildings on the night of **November 26, 2008** are seared into the collective memory of a nation — and its diaspora. But there's a story from that night that has never been told on screen. Until now.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=8n7bXkykd60</youtube>

**Bharat Bhagya Vidhata**, releasing this Thursday, June 12, is not about commandos or hostage negotiations. It's about the nurses of **Cama and Albless Hospital** who, while terrorists moved through the corridors, refused to abandon their patients. Over **400 people** survived that night because a group of women in scrubs decided they weren't going anywhere.

**Kangana Ranaut** plays the lead — a staff nurse, overlooked at home, underestimated at work, who becomes the spine of the hospital when everything collapses around her. It's the kind of role she gravitates toward: a woman underestimated by the world who turns out to be the most dangerous person in the room. Not dangerous with a gun. Dangerous with conviction.

> "This film is dedicated to those who shape India's destiny. The workers who make things with their hands — the Prime Minister named them Bharat Bhagya Vidhata. This touched our hearts, and we wanted to keep it as our title." — Kangana Ranaut

## The Night at Cama Hospital

What most people don't know — and what **director Manoj Tapadia** has spent years researching — is that Cama Hospital was one of the first targets hit on 26/11. Terrorists **Ajmal Kasab** and **Abu Ismail** entered the hospital after their rampage through Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus. Inside were hundreds of patients, many of them women recovering from surgeries and childbirth.

The film unfolds almost entirely within the hospital walls. No sweeping cityscapes. No military operations. Just corridors, wards, stairwells, and the people who held the line. Nurses barricading doors. Ward boys diverting attention. Security guards making split-second decisions that meant life or death for hundreds.

It's a contained thriller in the truest sense — closer to a survival film than a war movie. And it's the kind of story that the Indian film industry has inexplicably ignored for 18 years.

## Tax-Free Before It Even Opens

The film has already received a rare vote of confidence from the political establishment. **Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta** attended a red carpet premiere and immediately declared *Bharat Bhagya Vidhata* **tax-free in Delhi** — before the film had even opened to the public. She called it "outstanding" and said it would inspire children and families to learn about India's unsung heroes.

**BJP MP Bansuri Swaraj**, also present at the premiere, praised Kangana for "consistently selecting projects that honour India's unsung heroes and significant historical moments."

The ensemble cast backing Kangana is largely drawn from Marathi cinema's finest: **Girija Oak**, **Smita Tambe**, **Asha Shelar**, **Priya Berde**, **Suhita Thatte**, and **Rasika Agashe**. The title track, sung by **Sukhwinder Singh** and composed by **Aman Pant**, dropped this week — a rousing, patriotic anthem that sets the emotional register for what the film is trying to do.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For NRIs, 26/11 occupies a particular kind of anguish. Many watched it unfold on live television from thousands of miles away, unable to do anything, calling family members in Mumbai to check if they were safe. The Taj and Trident stories have been told — through documentaries, through *Hotel Mumbai*, through countless news features.

But the Cama Hospital story? The women who saved 400 lives while the world was watching smoke rise from the Taj? That story has been waiting. And now it arrives on June 12, competing for screens alongside **Imtiaz Ali's** *Main Vaapas Aaunga* and **Manoj Bajpayee's** *Governor* — a Thursday that will test how much emotional weight Bollywood can carry in a single day.

The nurses of Cama Hospital didn't make the front pages in 2008. Eighteen years later, they're getting a film. It's about time.
